task: To what extent was the Treaty of Versailles responsible for the rise of the Nazi Party in Germany? Use the sources provided and your own knowledge.
text:
The Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919, is often described as the starting point of Nazism, and Hitler himself spent most of his career attacking it. However, saying that the Treaty was responsible is too simple. In this essay I will argue that Versailles was an important long-term cause, because it gave extremists a grievance and a scapegoat, but that it only became decisive when the Great Depression destroyed the economic stability Germany had rebuilt in the mid-1920s. Without the Depression, I think the Nazis would have stayed a small fringe party.

The terms of the Treaty explain why many Germans felt humiliated. Germany lost about 13 percent of its territory and roughly 10 percent of its population, including Alsace-Lorraine and land given to Poland. The army was limited to 100,000 men, the Rhineland was demilitarised, and Article 231 made Germany accept responsibility for the war, which justified reparations that were fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks. Germany was not allowed to negotiate. Source A, the front page of the nationalist newspaper Deutsche Zeitung on the day of signing, which was headed "Vengeance, German nation!", shows how quickly the Treaty was presented as a national disgrace. Its origin matters here. It was published by a right-wing paper whose purpose was to stir up anger, so it tells us what the nationalist press wanted people to feel, not necessarily what the average German thought. Nevertheless, the word "Diktat" became common language, and this is useful evidence of how widely the resentment spread.

The Nazis exploited this resentment directly. The 1920 party programme demanded the abolition of the Treaty, and Hitler blamed it on the "November criminals", the politicians who had signed the armistice and then the Treaty. This was unfair, since the army leaders had told the government that the war could not be continued, but it worked as propaganda. More importantly for the long term, it tied the Weimar Republic to the Treaty in the public mind. Democratic politicians were attacked as traitors, and Erzberger and Rathenau were murdered in 1921 and 1922 by nationalists. Versailles therefore damaged the legitimacy of democracy before the Nazis were strong, which made it easier for them later to say that democracy itself was a foreign imposition.

The economic effects are the strongest direct link between the Treaty and the crisis of 1923. When Germany missed a reparations payment in January 1923, France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr, the government encouraged passive resistance and paid the workers by printing money, and by November a loaf of bread cost billions of marks. Savings were wiped out, and the middle classes who lost them were later a major source of Nazi support. Source B, from the economist John Maynard Keynes, argues that the reparations were impossible to pay and would ruin Europe. Keynes is a valuable source because he was an adviser to the British Treasury at the conference and understood the figures. However, his book The Economic Consequences of the Peace was written in 1919 after he resigned in protest, and its purpose was to persuade the British public that the Treaty was wrong. Later historians such as Sally Marks have argued that Germany could have paid and that it paid far less than was demanded. If she is right, then the real economic damage was smaller than Keynes said, and the German belief that the Treaty was unbearable mattered more than its actual terms. This is a limitation of treating the Treaty as a simple cause: its effect depended on how it was perceived.

The most important evidence against the Treaty being enough on its own is the period from 1924 to 1929. With the Dawes Plan in 1924, American loans and Stresemann's diplomacy, including Locarno in 1925 and entry to the League in 1926, Germany became more stable. The Young Plan in 1929 reduced reparations again. Yet the Treaty had not changed, and the Nazis won only 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928. If Versailles alone explained Nazism, then support should have been high during these years. It was not.

The Depression changed this. Source C, a table of unemployment and Nazi votes, shows unemployment rising from about 1.4 million in 1928 to nearly 6 million in 1932, while the Nazi vote rose from 2.6 percent to 18.3 percent in 1930 and 37.3 percent in July 1932. The link looks very strong. However, a table like this only shows correlation, and the unemployment figures were collected by government offices that did not count everyone, so they are probably an underestimate. We also need to ask why the Depression produced Nazism in Germany but not in Britain or the United States, which also suffered badly. Part of the answer goes back to Versailles and its aftermath. Germany relied on American loans that were withdrawn in 1929, and the Republic already lacked the trust of many voters. So the Depression was the trigger, but the Treaty helped make Germany fragile enough for it to be dangerous.

Other causes also deserve weight. Hitler's speeches and Goebbels's propaganda used modern methods, the SA frightened opponents and the Nazis promised protection from communism. Most importantly, Hitler did not win power by an election victory. The Nazi vote fell to 33 percent in November 1932, and he became Chancellor in January 1933 because Hindenburg and Papen believed they could control him. This was a political mistake by a small group of conservatives, and it cannot be blamed on a treaty signed fourteen years earlier.

In conclusion, the Treaty of Versailles was responsible for the rise of Nazism to a considerable but not a decisive extent. It created a lasting grievance, weakened the Republic and gave Hitler his main theme, so I would call it a necessary background condition. However, the events of 1929 to 1933, the Depression and the decisions of Germany's elites, were what turned that grievance into power. A limitation of my analysis is that my sources are mostly from newspapers and economists, so I have little evidence of what ordinary voters actually thought about the Treaty.

task: To what extent has the Three Gorges Dam brought more benefits than costs to China? Use the sources and your own knowledge.
text:
The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River in Hubei province is the largest hydroelectric project in the world. Construction began in 1994 and the dam was fully working by 2012. In this essay I will assess whether its benefits for China are greater than its costs. I will argue that the benefits are larger at a national level, especially for energy and flood control, but that the costs fall unfairly on local people and the environment, so the answer depends on whose perspective is used.

The first benefit is electricity. The dam has a capacity of 22.5 gigawatts and produces roughly 90 to 100 billion kilowatt hours a year. China relies heavily on coal, which causes air pollution and climate change, and according to the China Three Gorges Corporation this electricity replaces tens of millions of tonnes of coal each year. This helps the government's aim of cutting emissions, and it supplies power to fast-growing cities such as Shanghai and Wuhan. However, Source A, which gives these figures, was published by the company that runs the dam. It has a reason to present the dam as successful, so the numbers about coal saved may be exaggerated. I think the electricity benefit is real, but it should be treated as an estimate.

The second benefit is flood control. The Yangtze has flooded many times, and in 1998 floods affected over 200 million people and killed thousands. The dam has a flood storage space of about 22 billion cubic metres, so it can hold back water in the wet season. In 2020, when there were serious floods in southern China, the dam stored large amounts of water and protected cities downstream. Ships can also now travel further inland because the locks make the river deeper, so shipping costs have fallen. These are clear economic benefits for millions of people living along the river.

On the other hand, the costs are large. About 1.3 million people had to be moved from their homes, including whole towns such as Fengjie. Many were given compensation and new apartments, but Source B, an interview with a resettled farmer reported by a human rights group, says that some were given poor land and could not find jobs. This source is useful because it gives the personal view of someone affected, but it is only one person and the group that published it is critical of the government, so it may have picked the most negative story. Even so, other reports also mention corruption in compensation payments, so I think the problem is probably real.

There are also environmental costs. The reservoir is about 600 km long and has flooded forests and farmland, and over a thousand archaeological sites. Sediment is trapped behind the dam, which means less soil reaches the delta at Shanghai and the coast is eroding. The baiji river dolphin was declared functionally extinct in 2006, though overfishing and boat traffic were also causes, so the dam cannot take all the blame. There have also been landslides around the reservoir because the water level goes up and down. In addition, the government has admitted some of these problems, which makes the criticism more believable.

Weighing these up, the benefits are mainly national and economic, and the costs are mainly local and environmental. From the point of view of the Chinese government, the dam has been a success, because it gives power and protects against floods. From the point of view of the people who were moved, or fishermen and farmers downstream, the costs may be more important. Another factor is time. Floods and sediment problems may get worse in the future, while the energy benefit will last as long as the dam works, so it is hard to judge now.

In conclusion, I believe that the Three Gorges Dam has brought more benefits than costs to China as a whole, but only to a moderate extent, since the costs are serious and some are permanent, such as lost heritage and extinct species. The sources I used were limited, because the best figures come from the dam company and the criticisms come from campaign groups, so a more independent study of the sediment and resettlement would make my judgement stronger.

task: Evaluate the impact of a minimum wage on workers and on businesses. Refer to the sources provided and examples.
text:
A minimum wage is the lowest amount of money that an employer is allowed to pay a worker for each hour of work. Many countries have one, for example the United Kingdom, which introduced a national minimum wage in 1999. In this essay I am going to evaluate the impact of the minimum wage on workers and also on businesses and say whether it is a good thing or not.

First of all, the minimum wage is good for workers. It means that workers get paid more money so they can afford to buy the things they need like food, rent and clothes. Without a minimum wage some bosses could pay very low wages and workers would not have enough money to live on. This is why many people think it is a good policy. Workers who earn more money are also happier and they work harder, so this is good for the business as well. Another advantage is that it can reduce poverty because people at the bottom of society get a raise. In the UK the minimum wage has gone up many times since it was started and now many workers get over ten pounds an hour. This shows that the government wants to help workers.

Source A is an article that says that the minimum wage helps low paid workers and that it did not cause as much unemployment as people feared. This source is useful because it gives facts about the minimum wage in the UK. It says that after 1999 unemployment did not go up very much. So this shows that the minimum wage is a good idea and it works.

However, there are also disadvantages of the minimum wage for businesses. When the minimum wage goes up, businesses have to pay their workers more money and this increases their costs. Small businesses such as cafes and shops might find it difficult to pay this, because they do not make a lot of profit. If they cannot pay they might have to fire some of their workers, which means more unemployment. Some economists say that if the wage is set above what the market would pay, then there will be a surplus of labour, because more people want jobs but businesses want fewer workers. This is shown on a supply and demand diagram. Also the businesses might put up their prices to pay for the higher wages so the customers have to pay more, and this causes inflation. So the minimum wage is not always good.

Source B says that a minimum wage can lead to job losses, and that young people are the most affected. This is another view and it is a bit different from Source A. This source is also useful because it shows the other side. However, we do not know who wrote it so it could be unreliable.

Another thing is that some businesses might decide to use machines instead of people, which is called automation. For example, supermarkets now have self-checkouts, and this might be because of the cost of paying people. This means that the workers lose out. On the other hand, some businesses can afford the minimum wage because they are big, like Tesco and McDonalds, so it depends on the size of the business.

Also it is important to think about different countries. In some developing countries the minimum wage is very low and it is not always followed by the businesses, so workers still do not get enough. In countries like Bangladesh the garment workers have protested to get a higher wage. So the minimum wage is not always working in every country and it depends on whether the government makes sure it is followed.

In my opinion the minimum wage is mostly good because it helps the workers and the disadvantages for businesses are not that big. Businesses can solve the problem by raising prices a little, and because workers have more money they will spend it in shops, so it will come back to the businesses. This is called the multiplier effect. So both workers and businesses benefit in the end. Some people disagree and say that the minimum wage causes unemployment, but I think that is not a big problem because the evidence in Source A says that unemployment did not go up.

To conclude, the minimum wage has both positive and negative impacts on workers and on businesses. It helps workers earn more and reduces poverty, but it also makes costs higher for businesses and might cause unemployment. Overall I think it is a good policy and governments should have one. It is something that is very important in the world today, and many people have different opinions about it. There are many things that governments can do to help workers and businesses and the minimum wage is one of the most important ones. If the minimum wage is set at the right level, then it can be good for the economy, for the workers and for the businesses, and this is why I think most countries should have one and should make sure that it is followed.

task: To what extent was the United States responsible for the start of the Cold War? Use the sources and your own knowledge.
text:
The Cold War was a war between the USA and the Soviet Union after the Second World War. It was called cold because they did not actually fight each other with weapons. I think that the USA was responsible for the Cold War but also the USSR was a bit as well.

After the war ended in 1945 there was a meeting at Yalta and then Potsdam where Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin talked about what to do with Germany. Roosevelt died and then Truman became president and he did not like Stalin. Truman dropped the atomic bomb on Japan in 1945 and this made Stalin scared because America had the bomb and he did not. So that is one reason the USA was responsible.

Then in 1947 Truman made the Truman Doctrine which said that America would help any country that was fighting against communism. This made the Soviets angry. Then America gave Marshall Aid to Europe which was lots of money to rebuild Europe, but the Soviets said it was dollar imperialism. Stalin made the countries of Eastern Europe become communist and he put up the iron curtain. Churchill said this in a speech in 1946.

In 1948 there was the Berlin Blockade where Stalin stopped all the food from going into Berlin and America had to fly it in with planes, which was called the Berlin Airlift. This lasted for about a year. Then NATO was made in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955. So both sides were making alliances against each other. Source A is a cartoon and it shows that the Soviets are bad because they are taking over lots of countries. This source is useful because it shows what people thought at the time.

After that there was the Korean war and the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962 when Khrushchev put missiles on Cuba and Kennedy said he would invade. They nearly had a nuclear war but they did a deal in the end.

In conclusion the USA was to blame for the Cold War because of the atomic bomb and the Truman Doctrine but Stalin was also to blame because he took over Eastern Europe. It was a very bad time and a lot of people were scared. Both sides were responsible so you cannot say it was only one.

task: Carry out an independent investigation on a geographical or economic question of your choice. State your research question, explain why it matters, plan your action, use appropriate methods to collect information, and evaluate your process and results.
text:
Research question and rationale

To what extent has the 25 fils charge on single-use carrier bags changed the way shoppers use bags at three supermarkets in my neighbourhood in Dubai?

I chose this question because I notice that people at my local supermarket still ask for bags, even though a charge has applied in Dubai since July 2022. The charge is meant to reduce plastic waste, but 25 fils is very small, and economics suggests that a price this low might not change behaviour much. The question is geographical because it concerns human impact on the environment, and it is economic because it tests whether a small price signal changes demand. It matters because the government is moving towards a full ban on single-use bags, and if a small charge did not work, then the ban would be the only effective policy. I limited the question to three supermarkets and to one residential area so that I could collect enough first-hand data in the time available.

Action plan

I planned the work over four weeks. In week one I read background material and designed my methods, and I tested my questionnaire on four classmates, which showed me that my first draft asked two questions in one. In week two I carried out observations at three supermarkets, a large chain store, a medium store and a small store near the metro. In week three I gave a short questionnaire to shoppers. In week four I analysed my data and compared it with secondary sources. I decided to do observations at two different times, weekday evenings and Saturday mornings, because shopping habits could differ between a quick after-work trip and a big weekly shop.

Methods

I used three methods so that each could check the others. First, I counted bags. At each store I stood near the exit for 30 minutes at each time and recorded whether each shopper left with reusable bags, bought single-use bags, or carried no bag. I observed 120 shoppers in total. Second, I gave a questionnaire to 40 shoppers who agreed, with four short questions about how often they bring their own bag, whether the charge changed their behaviour, and the main reason. I asked permission from the managers first, and I did not record names. Third, I used secondary sources: a Dubai Municipality press release about the charge, and a 2023 report by an environmental group on bag use in the UAE. I judged these sources by their origin and purpose. The press release comes from the organisation that introduced the policy, so I expected it to emphasise success. The report is from a campaigning group, so it might emphasise problems.

Results

Of the 120 shoppers I observed, 79 (66 percent) used reusable bags, 18 (15 percent) bought single-use bags and 23 (19 percent) carried goods without any bag. Reusable use was highest at the large chain (74 percent) and lowest at the small store (52 percent). Saturday shoppers were more likely to bring bags than weekday shoppers (72 percent compared with 60 percent). In the questionnaire, 28 of 40 people said that the charge had changed their behaviour, but only 9 said the environment was their main reason, while 19 said they did not want to pay, and 12 said it was a habit now. The press release claimed a large fall in bag use after the charge, and my results are consistent with this, but I cannot confirm the size because I did not have bag counts from before July 2022.

Evaluation of process and results

My results suggest that the charge has changed behaviour for most shoppers, but mainly because of cost and habit and less because of environmental concern. This fits the economic idea that even a small price can change demand when the alternative is free and easy, since a reusable bag costs nothing once owned. However, the 25 fils figure is small, so I think the habit effect is also important, which my data cannot separate from the price effect.

There are several limitations. My sample was small, and 40 questionnaires is not enough to generalise about Dubai. I used convenience sampling, so people who agreed to answer may be more environmentally aware, and some may have given answers they thought I wanted to hear, which is social desirability bias. Observing at only three stores in one area, which is relatively wealthy, means my results may not represent other neighbourhoods. I also made observations during only two time periods, and I recorded shoppers who bought bags but could not tell whether some bought them for another use, such as bin liners. Lastly, I had no "before" data, so I could not measure change directly, only the present situation.

If I did this again, I would use a larger sample at more stores in different income areas, and I would look for older bag-use figures from a store or the municipality. I would also add a question asking whether people would still bring bags if the charge disappeared. Despite these limits, combining observation, a questionnaire and evaluated secondary sources let me check my findings against each other, and this made my conclusion more reliable than relying on one method.

task: Carry out an independent investigation on a question of your choice. State your research question, explain why it matters, plan your action, use appropriate methods to collect information, and evaluate your process and results.
text:
Research question

Has tourism helped or harmed the people of Bali?

Why I chose this

I chose this topic because I went to Bali on holiday with my family two years ago and I saw lots of tourists on the beaches and also many local people selling things. I wanted to find out if tourism is good for the local people or not. This is important because lots of countries rely on tourism and it can change the lives of local people. It is also a topic in geography because we studied tourism in class this term.

Action plan

First I made a list of what I needed to find out: the benefits of tourism in Bali, the problems of tourism, and what local people think. I gave myself three weeks. In the first week I looked for information on the internet. In the second week I did a questionnaire and interviewed my aunt, who has visited Bali many times. In the third week I put everything together and wrote my conclusion. I used a table to keep notes about each source so I would not lose track of them.

Methods

I used four sources. The first was a website called Bali Tourism Board which has statistics about how many tourists visit each year, and it says that about 6 million tourists visited in 2019 and that tourism provides most of the jobs on the island. The second was a National Geographic article about the problems of waste and water shortages in Bali. The third was a questionnaire which I gave to 15 of my classmates, asking whether they thought tourism was good or bad for local people. The fourth was an interview with my aunt who spoke to hotel workers and taxi drivers on her visits.

I checked if my sources were reliable. The Bali Tourism Board website is reliable because it is an official website and has lots of numbers. The National Geographic article is reliable because it is by a well known magazine. My aunt is useful because she has been to Bali lots of times, but she is a tourist so she might not know everything.

Results

From the websites I found that tourism gives jobs to many people in Bali, in hotels, restaurants and transport, and that it brings in a lot of money. I also found that tourism causes problems such as plastic waste on the beaches, and that hotels and pools use a lot of water so that local farmers have less. Prices of land also go up so local people cannot afford to buy it. In the questionnaire, 10 out of 15 classmates said tourism was mainly good and 5 said it was mainly bad. My aunt said that the people she met were happy to have jobs but some said they were worried about the traffic and rubbish.

Evaluation

My conclusion is that tourism has helped Bali more than it has harmed it, because it gives jobs and money, but it also causes some problems which the government must solve. I think my investigation went well because I found out lots of information from different places. One problem was that my questionnaire was only given to my classmates who have never lived in Bali, so it does not show what local people think. Also I only had one interview. If I did the investigation again I would try to contact someone in Bali, for example by email, or look for more sources that were written by Balinese people. I also think I should have planned my time better because I did the questionnaire at the end, so I did not have time to do more.

task: Carry out an independent investigation on a question of your choice. State your research question, explain why it matters, plan your action, use appropriate methods to collect information, and evaluate your process and results.
text:
Research question: How does social media affect teenagers?

I chose this question because I use social media a lot and so do my friends. I think it is a very important topic in the world today because many teenagers spend a lot of time on their phones.

My plan was to look on the internet and find out some information about social media and teenagers. Then I would write down what I found and write a conclusion.

For my research I looked at some websites like Google and some articles. I found out that teenagers spend about 7 hours a day on social media. Some websites said that social media is bad for mental health because teenagers compare themselves to other people and get anxious. Other websites said that social media is good because you can talk to your friends and learn new things. I also asked three of my friends what they thought and they said it was both good and bad.

The websites that I used were reliable because they came up on the first page of Google. I did not write down the names of all of them.

My conclusion is that social media has good and bad effects on teenagers. It depends on how much you use it. I think I did well because I found a lot of information. Next time I could find more websites and ask more people.

task: Present your research on the following question: Has the fast fashion industry done more good than harm in Bangladesh? Include your research question, plan, methods, findings and evaluation.
text:
Slide 1
Fast Fashion in Bangladesh: More Good or More Harm?
An individuals and societies investigation
Year 5 | Geography and Economics

Slide 2
Research question
To what extent has the fast fashion industry done more good than harm for people in Bangladesh?
Focus: workers, the economy, the environment

Slide 3
Why does it matter?
- Bangladesh is the 2nd largest clothing exporter in the world
- Clothes in my wardrobe are labelled "Made in Bangladesh"
- Consumers in richer countries make choices that affect workers abroad

Slide 4
Action plan
Week 1: background reading and key terms
Week 2: find primary and secondary sources
Week 3: survey of 25 students
Week 4: analysis and presentation

Slide 5
Methods and sources
- World Bank report on Bangladesh's economy
- Clean Clothes Campaign report on wages
- Article about Rana Plaza (BBC News)
- Survey results: 15 of 25 said they would pay a little more, but fewer said they actually check labels
- Survey: "Would you pay more for ethically made clothes?" (25 students)
Figure 1: Methods used and what each gave me

Slide 6
Background
- Garment industry started growing in the 1980s
- About 80% of export earnings
- About 4 million workers, around 60% women
- Key terms: export-led growth, multiplier effect, sweatshop
- Brands such as H&M and Zara order large quantities at very low prices, so factories compete on cost
- Main sources of growth: cheap labour, trade preferences from the EU
Figure 2: map of Bangladesh showing Dhaka and garment zones

Slide 7
The good
- Jobs for millions of people, especially women with few other options
- Women gain income and independence
- Growth: GDP has grown about 6% a year before 2020
- Minimum wage raised from 5,300 taka (2013) to 8,000 taka (2018) and 12,500 taka (2023)

Slide 8
The harm
- Rana Plaza collapse, 2013: 1,134 workers died
- Wages still below a living wage
- Long hours, unsafe factories, limited union rights
- Pollution of rivers from textile dyes

Slide 9
Different perspectives
- Factory owners: need low prices because brands demand cheap clothes
- Workers: want jobs but also safety and higher pay
- Brands and consumers: profit and cheap fashion
- Government: needs exports for development
- Environmental groups: want cleaner dyeing and water treatment
The harm and the good are experienced very differently depending on who you are

Slide 10
Evaluating my sources
- World Bank: reliable data but promotes development, may focus on growth
- Clean Clothes Campaign: detailed but an NGO with a campaign aim
- BBC: factual, but about one event
- My survey: only 25 students, biased sample

Slide 11
Conclusion
- Good: jobs, income, economic growth
- Harm: danger, low pay, pollution
- I think it has done more good than harm overall, but only because the Accord on Fire and Building Safety (2013) improved safety
- The benefits are not shared fairly

Evaluation and bibliography
- Limits: no interviews with workers, small survey
- Next time: contact an NGO, compare with Vietnam

Thank you. Any questions?

task: To what extent was Mikhail Gorbachev responsible for the collapse of the Soviet Union? Use the sources and your own knowledge.
text:
Mikhail Gorbachev was the last leader of the Soviet Union and his time in power was very important in the history of the twentieth century. In this essay I will talk about what Gorbachev did and what happened to the Soviet Union while he was in power, and then I will say how responsible he was for the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Mikhail Gorbachev was born on 2 March 1931 in a village called Privolnoye in the south of Russia. His family were farmers. He studied law at Moscow State University and he joined the Communist Party in 1952. He worked his way up in the party and in 1978 he became a member of the Central Committee and in 1980 he joined the Politburo. When Leonid Brezhnev died in 1982, Yuri Andropov took over, and then Andropov died in 1984 and Konstantin Chernenko took over. Chernenko died in March 1985 and then on 11 March 1985 Gorbachev became General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. He was only 54 years old, which was young compared with the old leaders before him.

When Gorbachev became leader the Soviet Union had many problems. The economy was not growing very fast and there were shortages of food and goods in the shops. The Soviet Union was also fighting a war in Afghanistan, which had started in December 1979. The war was very expensive and many Soviet soldiers were dying. Also the arms race with the United States was costing a lot of money, and the American president Ronald Reagan had started a big build up of weapons in the 1980s. In April 1986 there was a disaster at the nuclear power station in Chernobyl in Ukraine, which exploded on 26 April. The government did not tell people about it at first and this made people trust the government less.

In 1985 and 1986 Gorbachev introduced his new policies. The first was called perestroika, which means restructuring, and the second was called glasnost, which means openness. Perestroika was about changing the economy and glasnost was about letting people say what they thought. In 1987 he allowed some private businesses called cooperatives. In 1988 there was a new law on state enterprises. In 1989 there were the first partly free elections to the Congress of People's Deputies, which was held in March 1989. Many people voted against the communist candidates.

In 1987 Gorbachev met Reagan and they signed the INF Treaty on 8 December 1987 in Washington, which got rid of medium range nuclear missiles. In February 1989 the Soviet army left Afghanistan. In 1988 Gorbachev made a speech at the United Nations in December where he said that the Soviet Union would cut its army by half a million men, and that countries could choose their own way. This was a very important speech.

Then in 1989 there were revolutions in Eastern Europe. In June 1989 the Poles voted in elections and Solidarity won. In August the Hungarians opened their border with Austria. In October 1989 there were big protests in East Germany, in Leipzig and Berlin, and on 9 November 1989 the Berlin Wall was opened. After that, in December, the communist governments in Czechoslovakia and Romania fell. In Romania the leader Ceausescu was shot on Christmas Day. Gorbachev did not send in the army to stop these revolutions like previous leaders had done in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968. Source A is a photograph of people dancing on the Berlin Wall. It shows that people were happy and that the Wall had come down.

In 1990 more things happened. In March 1990 Gorbachev was made President of the Soviet Union and the Communist Party gave up its monopoly of power. Lithuania declared independence on 11 March 1990. In June 1990 Boris Yeltsin was elected as the President of the Russian republic, and he declared that Russia's laws were more important than Soviet laws. In October 1990 Gorbachev got the Nobel Peace Prize. Germany became united again on 3 October 1990. Meanwhile the economy was getting worse and there were long queues for bread and other goods, and prices were going up.

In 1991 there were more events. In January 1991 Soviet troops attacked people in Lithuania and Latvia, and some people were killed. In March 1991 there was a referendum where most people voted to keep the Soviet Union, but six republics did not take part. In June 1991 Yeltsin was elected President of Russia in a popular vote. Gorbachev wanted to make a new treaty that would give the republics more power, and it was going to be signed on 20 August 1991.

Then on 19 August 1991 there was a coup. A group of hardline communists, who were called the Gang of Eight, put Gorbachev under house arrest at his holiday home in Crimea at Foros. They were the vice president Gennady Yanayev, the KGB head Vladimir Kryuchkov, the defence minister Dmitry Yazov and others. They wanted to stop the new treaty. Yeltsin stood on a tank outside the Russian parliament, which was called the White House, and made a speech against the coup. After three days the coup failed and Gorbachev came back to Moscow on 22 August. But Gorbachev was now much weaker and Yeltsin was stronger. Source B is a picture of Yeltsin standing on the tank and it shows that he was brave.

After the coup the republics wanted to leave the Soviet Union. Ukraine declared independence on 24 August 1991 and in December 1991 there was a referendum in Ukraine where over 90 percent voted for independence. Many other republics such as Estonia, Latvia, Georgia and Belarus also declared independence. On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus met in Belovezha forest and signed an agreement that said the Soviet Union did not exist anymore and they made the Commonwealth of Independent States. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned as President on television and the red flag with the hammer and sickle was taken down from the Kremlin. The next day, 26 December, the Soviet Union was officially dissolved.

So these are the main events in the story of the end of the Soviet Union. Gorbachev was a very important person in all of this. He was the leader when it all happened, and the policies that he introduced such as perestroika and glasnost changed the Soviet Union a lot. If he had not been the leader then maybe the Soviet Union would not have collapsed in 1991. He also did not use force to stop the revolutions in Eastern Europe, and this was important as well. Other people were also important such as Boris Yeltsin, who became the leader of Russia, and Ronald Reagan, who the Americans say won the Cold War.

In conclusion, Gorbachev was responsible for the collapse of the Soviet Union to a large extent because he was the leader and he introduced reforms, and the things that happened while he was in power led to the end of the Soviet Union. However there were also other reasons such as the economy, the war in Afghanistan and Yeltsin, so he was not the only reason. Gorbachev is a very interesting person in history, and he is remembered in different ways by different people. In the West he is remembered as a hero but in Russia many people do not like him because they think he destroyed their country. This is why the Soviet Union collapsed and it is a very important event in history.

task: Carry out an independent investigation on a question of your choice. Explain your research question and why it matters, show your action plan, use appropriate methods to collect information, and evaluate your process and results. (Submitted for all four criteria.)
text:
Research question

How much does the price of bubble tea affect how often students at my school buy it?

Rationale

There are three bubble tea shops within ten minutes of our school and I see many students buying drinks after school. When one of the shops put up its prices last term, I noticed fewer people queuing. I wanted to find out whether price really changes how often students buy bubble tea, or whether they buy it whatever the price is. This matters because it tells us something about how sensitive customers are to price, and because many students spend a large part of their pocket money on it. I limited my investigation to students in Years 9 to 11 at my school so that my sample could be reached in two weeks.

Action plan

Week 1: design a questionnaire and test it with five friends, then change the unclear questions. Week 2: give the questionnaire to students in each year group and record the shop prices myself by visiting the three shops. Week 3: put the results in tables and graphs and look for patterns. Week 4: write up and evaluate. I kept a log in my planner each day so that I could remember what I had done and change my plan. For example, I originally planned to ask 100 students, but after the first two days I saw that I could only get about 60 because of exams, so I changed my target.

Methods

I used a questionnaire as my main method because I needed opinions and habits from many people. It had six questions, including how many bubble teas the student buys each week, the usual price they pay, and what they would do if the price went up by 5 dirhams. I used closed questions with choices so that the answers could be counted easily, and one open question asking why they chose their favourite shop. I chose students from each year group by asking in the corridor and at lunch, with a roughly equal number from each year. I also visited the three shops on two different days to record their prices, because I wanted to check what students said against real prices. Finally, I interviewed the manager of the nearest shop for ten minutes, asking whether sales had changed after the price rise. I asked for permission first and I wrote the notes straight afterwards.

Results

I collected 58 completed questionnaires. The average number of bubble teas bought was 1.7 per week. The usual price was between 14 and 18 dirhams. When asked what they would do if the price rose by 5 dirhams, 29 students (50 percent) said they would buy less often, 17 (29 percent) said they would change to a cheaper shop, and 12 (21 percent) said it would make no difference. Year 11 students said they would be less affected than Year 9 students, which may be because older students have more pocket money. The favourite shop was usually chosen because of taste and distance from school, and only 8 students mentioned price as the main reason. The manager said sales dropped slightly for about two weeks after the price rise and then returned to normal.

Evaluation of the process

The combination of a questionnaire, price checks and an interview helped me to compare different kinds of evidence, and the interview supported the idea that the effect is short. The questionnaire worked well because the pilot test made the questions clearer. However, there are limitations. My sample of 58 is small, and it was a convenience sample, so students who were in the corridor may not represent all students. People may have said what they would do, but this is different from what they really do. I also had to rely on what students said they spend, and some may not remember exactly. I also only had one interview, and a manager might not want to say that sales fell. In addition, I recorded the prices at only two moments. If I repeated the investigation I would keep a record of sales over several months, and I would ask more students and spread out the days when I asked them. Overall, I think my methods fitted the question and I was able to adapt my plan when problems appeared, but a bigger sample would make the findings stronger.

task: To what extent was the Black Death responsible for the end of feudalism in England? Use the sources and your own knowledge. (Submitted for all four criteria.)
text:
The Black Death arrived in England in 1348 and killed somewhere between a third and a half of the population. Feudalism was the system in which peasants worked the land for a lord in return for protection and a place to live. In this essay I will argue that the Black Death was a very important cause of the decline of feudalism, but that it was not the only cause, because tensions already existed before 1348 and changes continued long afterwards.

The most direct effect of the plague was a shortage of labour. With so many peasants dead, landowners could not find workers to farm their land, and survivors could demand higher wages or move to another lord who would pay more. This broke the idea that a peasant was tied to one manor. The government reacted with the Ordinance of Labourers in 1349 and the Statute of Labourers in 1351, which tried to fix wages at their pre-plague level. Source A, a statute of this kind, shows how worried the ruling class was. It is useful because it comes from the government at the time, but it only shows what the government wanted to happen. The fact that the laws were passed again and again suggests they were not being obeyed, so the labour shortage was probably serious and workers were ignoring the rules.

As a result, many lords moved away from farming their land directly with serfs. Instead they rented out land for money to tenants, which is called leasing, and the serfs gradually became free tenants. Commutation, where services were replaced by payments, had begun before the plague, but it sped up after 1349. By 1400 serfdom had become much less common in many parts of England, although it did not disappear completely. This supports the view that the Black Death changed the system, but I would say that it accelerated a change that was already happening, rather than starting it.

The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 shows how the plague changed attitudes. The immediate cause was the poll tax of 1380 and 1381, which was a new tax on every adult to pay for the war in France. Peasants from Kent and Essex marched on London, led by Wat Tyler and encouraged by the priest John Ball, who said "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?" The rebels wanted an end to serfdom and a fixed rent of 4 pence an acre. Source B, a chronicle by Jean Froissart, describes the rebels as wild and violent. However, Froissart was a supporter of the nobles, who wrote about events he did not see, so his account is likely to be biased against the peasants. Because the peasants were wealthier and more confident after the plague, they were prepared to demand their rights, and this makes the Black Death an indirect cause of the revolt.

Nevertheless, the revolt did not directly end feudalism. It was crushed, Wat Tyler was killed at Smithfield and the king, Richard II, broke his promise to abolish serfdom. This shows that the lords still had power in 1381. So it would be wrong to say that the Black Death immediately ended feudalism.

Other factors also weakened the system. The Hundred Years War, which started in 1337, led to heavy taxation and, because it was fought with paid soldiers and archers, reduced the need for knights who held land in return for military service. Also, the growth of towns and trade meant that more people had money, and some serfs escaped to towns, where the saying went that "town air makes you free". The influence of the Church was also falling, with John Wycliffe criticising its wealth. These changes meant that the feudal system was already under strain. In my view, the plague was the strongest cause because it affected every manor at once, while the other causes were slower or limited to some regions.

Finally, we should think about different perspectives. Lords lost income and tried to hold on to their power through laws, while peasants gained bargaining power and often better living standards, with more meat and bread in their diet. Historians have debated this. Some, like Marxist historians, see the plague as the cause of a class struggle, whereas others emphasise the longer decline of manorial farming.

In conclusion, the Black Death was responsible for the end of feudalism to a large extent, because it caused a labour shortage that changed the relationship between lords and peasants permanently. However, it was not the sole cause, because commutation and the war with France were already weakening the system, and feudalism ended slowly over a century or more. The best explanation is that the plague combined with these earlier trends to make a change that was probably coming anyway much faster.
